name: Finnish sauna horn cupping

image.caption: Indian cupping horns of horn and copper Wellcome M0020070

lead: Finnish cupping (kuppaus) is a traditional treatment in which cups are placed on the warmed skin and small cuts are made so blood is drawn out. Historically the cups were hollowed cattle horns with a membrane over a hole in the tip; modern practitioners use sterilisable silicone cups.

Practitioners and clients describe it as a treatment for pain and circulation. Within appearance and training circles the interest is recovery and muscle comfort, which feeds into training. Reviews of cupping in general describe low-quality evidence.

paras: The body is warmed, usually in a sauna, the skin is disinfected, cups go on trigger or acupressure points, small incisions are made, and blood drains for a time before the cups come off. Today this is typically done in a treatment room with trained therapists.

Bruising, burns, scarring and skin darkening are reported for cupping generally, and wet cupping carries infection risk if equipment is not sterile. Finnish practitioners use client questionnaires, liability insurance and hygiene rules.

angle.text: Practitioners use the treatment for sore, tight muscles. The route to better looks is through recovery and more comfortable training.

lead: Finnish blood cupping (kuppaus) is a traditional treatment in which cups create suction over small skin incisions so that blood is drawn out; it has long been connected with the sauna, where the body is warmed first [1]. Wikipedia notes that Finnish wet cupping, done in saunas since the 15th century, used cattle-horn cups with a valve to create suction [2].

Historical cups were cut and hollowed cattle horns sealed with a membrane, with a small hole in the membrane letting air escape so the seal held; cuts were made with knives or iron cupping axes [1]. Modern practitioners use heat-resistant silicone cups and sterile blades [1].

Practitioners describe the purpose as relieving pain and improving circulation [1]. For readers interested in how they look, the draw is muscle relaxation and recovery from training, and the skin appearance after a session.

paras: The sequence described by the Finnish living-heritage wiki is: warm the body, clean the skin, place cups on points, cut under the cups, drain blood, remove cups and disinfect, followed by rest and fluids [1]. This is a summary of the tradition, not a protocol.

Records of cupping stretch back thousands of years, and in Finland written references date to the mid-16th century; the last home medical book with cupping instructions was published in 1907 [1]. Traditional belief held that illness resided in 'bad blood' and that removing it was beneficial [1]. Knowledge passed down through families, often from mother to daughter [1].

No studies found on horn cupping specifically. Reviews of cupping in general report low-to-moderate evidence for reducing musculoskeletal pain, with possible placebo-level benefit and generally poor study quality [2].

Cupping in general can cause petechiae, bruising, scarring, burns and skin discolouration [2]. In Finland practitioners use a signed client questionnaire, carry liability insurance and follow hygiene guidance from the supervisory authority Valvira [1].
